# Derive a deck from a deck

**Workflow:** [`tarot/tarot-deck-derive.json`](../tarot/tarot-deck-derive.json)

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Family | `tarot` |
| Nodes | 18 |
| Links | 25 |
| Paid API calls per run | **1 per input** |
| Reads | `tarot/anchors/deck` · `tarot/anchors/wands-courts` · `tarot/seed` |
| Writes | `tarot/derived` · `tarot/styles/hidden-light.json` |

---

A seed deck in, a new deck out, in a style you locked and can lock again a year from now.

**Manifest → Slot Loader → (Constraints + Style Lock + Scopes) → Resolve → generate → Frame → Lettering → Save**

## Run this before you run it

`scope` on the manifest is set to **proof set** — twelve cards chosen to exercise every scoping dimension: three majors, a complete court in one suit, a court in a *second* suit, and one number across all four suits and elements. That is enough to see whether the cascade is doing what you meant. Only then set `full deck`, which is 78 API calls with no partial billing.

## The cascade

Read it left to right. Each **Style Scope** adds one layer over a subset of the deck, and **later wins** — the rightmost node that matches a card is the specific one. That is the whole ordering rule; there is no hidden specificity calculation, because chain order is something you can see and specificity is something you would have to reason about.

Layers combine differently by kind, deliberately:

- **Text accumulates.** A Wands court gets the deck's prose, then the courts' prose, then its own. It refines; it does not replace.
- **Anchors do not.** The most specific matching set leads the plate and the deck's own anchors backfill the remaining tiles — so a suit's courts read like each other first and like the deck second.
- **Fidelity overrides.** Any axis left at **-1** inherits from the layer before, so a scope can change structure alone and leave everything else where the deck put it.

## Anchors

`anchor_dir` is a folder of cards you have already approved. Use **several deliberately unalike ones** — a major, a pip, a court. A single anchor is the failure mode here: the whole deck starts inheriting its composition rather than its style. They are composited into one plate that occupies one reference slot, and a model shown several cards at once is likelier to read the style they share than to copy the one picture it was handed.

## The fidelity vector

Five axes, each **1.0 holds the seed card's version, 0.0 lets it change entirely**: `structure`, `style`, `colour`, `lighting`, `iconography`.

The named operations are points in that space, and any combination is just another point:

| | structure | style | colour | iconography |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| restyle | hold | free | free | hold |
| restructure | free | hold | hold | hold |
| re-symbolize | hold | hold | hold | **free** |
| retone | hold | hold | **free** | hold |

**How it reaches the model, honestly.** Stability has real parameters for this and the Resolve node emits them — `control_strength`, `composition_fidelity`, `style_strength`, `change_strength`, all per card. **The FLUX.2 API has none**: its schemas carry no control strength and no style weight, only `guidance` on flex. So over FLUX.2 the vector reaches the model as *prompt language plus which image sits in which reference slot*. That is reproducible and it composes, but it is soft where a local IPAdapter would be hard. The wording lives in **`phrases.json`** beside the pack — edit it, because the exact phrasing is the part worth tuning and tuning it should not mean editing Python.

## Constraints belong to the deck

"The Tower is red no matter what" is a fact about your deck, not about a style — so it sits next to the manifest and travels through every derivation. Swap the entire style lock and the constraints still land, last, after all style text. Hex codes written in a rule are read out and rendered into the plate as a swatch, because a model follows a swatch far more reliably than it follows hex in prose.

## Read the report

Resolve prints which layers each card ended up under, and flags any card that only ever matched the base layer. With several overlapping scopes across 78 cards you cannot hold that in your head, and a card that fell through every scope is exactly the one that will break cohesion.

The **Cohesion Report** at the end measures the finished deck — lightness and saturation against the deck's own median, plus whether the colour constraints were actually honoured. It costs nothing, so run it every time.

## Cost

One API call per card in scope. Fix the seed: it makes the run reproducible *and* cacheable, so re-queuing after changing only the border or the lettering costs nothing at all.
